title: How to raise attainment in mathematics
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton summarises a large randomised controlled trial of 2,901 Year 7 pupils across 20 UK schools, in which Eedi homework was compared with business-as-usual platforms such as Sparx and MathsWatch. The overall effect size was 0.17, about two months of extra progress, and it doubled for pupils who used it for 10 to 15 minutes each week. Rather than simply urging readers to adopt the product, he draws four lessons that apply to any homework or assessment platform. Homework should feed back into lessons, multiple-choice diagnostic questions reveal why pupils struggle, short frequent homework beats long infrequent homework, and well-run leaderboards can lift motivation. The strongest gains came from teachers who used the misconception data to shape whole-class feedback and small-group intervention.
points: Homework data only pays off when it visibly changes what happens in the next lesson, which also makes pupils take the homework seriously.
Diagnostic multiple-choice questions show why a pupil is stuck, and can be used in Do Nows, prerequisite checks and exit tickets as well as homework.
Splitting a long fortnightly homework into shorter weekly sessions raised completion in every school Barton has seen try it.
Leaderboards motivate best when they reward effort and improvement as well as raw attainment, so the same pupils are not always on top.
An active-control design, set against platforms schools already use, makes the reported gains more credible.
quotes: Our intervention groups used Eedi for their homework, whereas the control groups continued with business as usual, which for 89% of them meant using platforms like Sparx or MathsWatch. This makes the results particularly robust, as Eedi had to demonstrate its value against tools that schools are already using.
Getting students to participate in any homework, especially online homework, is challenging. I often visit schools where fewer than 20% of students complete their online assignments.

The teachers in our study who saw the greatest learning gains were those who used Eedi’s reporting insights in their lessons. They gave whole-class feedback on problematic questions or gathered specific students into small intervention groups based on shared misconceptions.

Long-time readers will know that I love a few things in life more than multiple-choice diagnostic questions. A good diagnostic question allows teachers to pinpoint precisely why students are struggling, not just that they are struggling.

You don’t have to use diagnostic questions for homework. You could use them as part of your Do Now, or to check prerequisite knowledge before teaching a new idea, or as part of an Exit Ticket to see what students have learned that lesson.

The teachers in our study who saw the greatest learning gains were those who got their students using Eedi for regular, short sessions. 10-15 minutes a week was the sweet spot. This felt manageable to students – as opposed to some epic 1-hour homework – meaning more students engaged.

Teachers in our study observed that leaderboards boosted student engagement. The key was to ensure that the same students were not always at the top, so focus was not only on achievement but also on effort and improvement.
